idiom_name: hand-rolled name -> value table (GHashTable or intrusive entry list) on the owner struct
implementation_notes: C has no dynamic member access, so the pattern is built from primitives: the owner struct carries a GHashTable (or an intrusive list of key/value entries) behind order_set/order_get/order_has/order_remove functions, and an iteration function provides discovery. GLib also attaches named data to objects whose type you cannot change - g_object_set_data stores a table of associations from strings to pointers per GObject and g_object_set_qdata does the same with an interned GQuark name. Descriptors must be hand-written (a static table of names, types and defaults) because nothing in the language reflects over values; the classic structure stays justified here because there is nothing to absorb it.
pitfalls: g_hash_table_lookup() cannot distinguish a missing key from a key whose value is NULL - use g_hash_table_lookup_extended() when absence must be reported.

Keys passed to g_object_set_data()/g_object_set_qdata() are interned as GQuarks and that table never shrinks (the docs advise keeping the key set small and bounded), so untrusted property names leak memory for the process's lifetime.

Ownership is manual: pass key and value destroy functions (g_hash_table_new_full, g_object_set_data_full) or every property leaks, and a typo'd key is just a silently empty slot because no compile-time check exists.
